Competing candidates either have weaker reported discrimination (e.g., PGS000740 AUROC 0.811 with an early-onset <50 endpoint mismatch; multiple PRSweb ‘lung and bronchus’ scores with AUROC ~0.52–0.54), are ancestry-/subpopulation-restricted (e.g., never-smoker EAS-only scores), or have missing/limited comparable metrics. However, the evidence remains sub-optimal because the reported AUROC/C-index for PGS000078 appears to be a full model with extensive covariates (including detailed smoking variables, family history, PM2.5, interaction terms), and no PRS-only AUROC/R2 is provided; thus the high AUROC may be substantially covariate-driven and is not cleanly comparable across models.

Direct-match candidates for lung cancer are present (35 models). Among broadly aligned endpoints, PGS000078 has strong concept/endpoint alignment (trait_reported: Lung cancer; trait_efo: lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported: Incident lung cancer) and large European validation (n=392,539) with reported discrimination (AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849) plus a per-SD effect size (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.11–1.22). Competing candidates have notable limitations: PGS000740 targets early-onset lung cancer (<50y), making it endpoint-restricted; several PRSweb lung/bronchus models show low AUROC (~0.52–0.54) or are broader composite endpoints; PGS004860 reports very high AUROC (0.893) but is from a specific French-Canadian case-control cohort with smaller validation (n=24,012) and provides only full-model metrics, reducing comparability. Confidence is not high because most candidates report only full-model AUROCs with varying covariate sets (often including smoking and related terms), and PRS-only/incremental metrics are largely missing, so the PRS contribution cannot be cleanly compared across models.

Multiple direct-match candidates exist for major depressive disorder, but several have endpoint/metric comparability issues that prevent a clearly definitive pick. I prefer PGS003578 because its phenotyping_reported is directly aligned to the target (“Major depressive disorder”), it comes from a coherent study family explicitly focused on improving MDD phenotyping (multiple closely related MDD PRSs released together), it uses only basic genetic ancestry covariates (PCs 1–10), and it shows the strongest reported R² within that family (0.0257, European validation; n=42,250), which is consistent with the domain-knowledge preference for endpoint-fidelity plus comparable performance among similar endpoints. Key limitation: many candidates report only full-model metrics (or non-comparable outcomes), and some high-looking metrics appear tied to mismatched endpoints (e.g., muscle pain in fluoxetine takers; brain imaging/volume outcomes) or time-to-event packaging; also, several non-family alternatives (e.g., PRSmixPlus PGS004760 incremental R²=0.024; PRS-CS-auto PGS003333 pseudo-R²=0.022) are close enough that the visible evidence does not fully separate them, so confidence is moderate rather than high.

Direct-match candidates are present for major depressive disorder, but the evidence is heterogeneous and several candidates have endpoint-mismatch issues or non-comparable/possibly inflated metrics. Among models with clearly aligned phenotyping_reported as major depressive disorder (generic disease status rather than treatment-specific, neuroimaging proxy, or medication-side-effect endpoints), the 2023 ‘Phenotype integration…’ cluster (PGS003576–PGS003585) provides the strongest coherent set: same study family, explicit MDD phenotype, EUR GWAS/DEV with EUR validation reported, and consistently reported R² values.
